o: Return false if any number is a prefix of another. With only 50 strings of length ≤ 50, almost anything works; the elegant trick is sorting: after lexicographic sort, any prefix relationship must occur between adjacent strings, because a prefix sorts immediately before its extensions.
k: Lexicographic sorting places every string directly before all of its extensions.
Therefore checking only adjacent pairs after sorting suffices — a single startswith test per pair.

a.i: If a is a prefix of b, then a ≤ b and nothing can sort strictly between them that breaks adjacency of some prefix pair; formally, if a is a prefix of c and a < b < c lexicographically, then a is also a prefix of b. So one linear adjacent scan finds any violation.
s: For each consecutive pair (a, b), if b.startsWith(a) return false.
a.t: O(n log n · L) — sorting dominates, L = max string length

a.n: Approach 2: Trie insertion with conflict detection
a.i: Insert each number into a trie. While inserting, if we pass a node flagged as the end of a previously inserted number, that earlier number is a prefix of the current one; if the final node already has children, the current number is a prefix of an earlier one. Either condition returns false.
s: Build a trie root; for each number walk/create children.
If any visited node is marked isEnd, return false.
After finishing, mark the last node isEnd; if it already had children, return false.
Return true if all insertions succeed.
a.t: O(total characters) — one trie pass per string

w: Sorting is the pragmatic interview answer (three lines); the trie generalizes to streaming inserts or when you must report which pair conflicts. Pitfall: comparing adjacent pairs is required — checking all pairs is O(n²L) and unnecessary. Edge cases: duplicate numbers (a number is a prefix of itself — the sorted check catches equal adjacent strings since startswith is true). Follow-up: return the conflicting pair, or handle numbers arriving online (trie wins).
